notes.front: What is the second Kanban practice, actively managing items in a workflow, in one sentence?
notes.back: Acting on the items already between started and finished, for example by controlling WIP, stopping items ageing unnecessarily and unblocking blocked work.
notes.explanation: The Guide says items in the workflow must be managed actively; defining and visualizing the workflow is not enough on its own.
notes.example: Like an air-traffic controller watching the planes already in the air, not just drawing up flight plans.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What is Work Item Age?
notes.back: The elapsed time between when a work item started and the current date.
notes.explanation: It applies only to unfinished items, so it shows which work is getting old while there is still time to act. It is one of the Guide's four mandatory flow metrics.
notes.example: An item started on Monday is three days old on Thursday, whether or not anyone worked on it on Tuesday.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Flow Metrics”, p. 7

notes.front: What is blocked work?
notes.back: Work items that have stopped (blocked or on hold), usually because they are waiting on someone or something inside or outside the team.
notes.explanation: Blocked items keep ageing while nothing moves, which is why the Guide lists unblocking blocked work as a form of active management.
notes.example: A change waiting three days for another team's sign-off is blocked: its age grows while no work happens.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Unblocking Blocked Work”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a pull system in Kanban?
notes.back: A system where work on an item starts (is pulled or selected) only when there is a clear signal of capacity for it.
notes.explanation: The Guide says controlling WIP should create a pull system as an effect.
notes.example: Like a café that takes the next order off the rail only when a barista is free, instead of every barista juggling five drinks.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What is a WIP limit?
notes.back: A cap on the board, as a number or fixed places (slots or tokens), on one column, several grouped columns or the whole board.
notes.explanation: Slots or tokens are places that items must occupy. It is one common way to control WIP. The December 2020 Guide named it; the May 2025 Guide no longer uses the term and allows any representation.
notes.example: A “3” above the Test column: a fourth item may not enter Test until one leaves.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (December 2020), “Controlling Work in Progress”, p. 6

notes.front: What is right-sizing a work item, according to the Kanban Pocket Guide?
notes.back: Checking, before pulling an item in, that it can likely finish within the SLE's time; if not, splitting or redefining it first.
notes.explanation: It is not same-sizing: variation in item size always exists, and items only need to fit within the range the SLE describes.
notes.example: With an SLE of “85% in 12 days or less”, the team asks of each new item: can we finish this in 12 days or less?
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Right Sizing Redux”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Kanban Pocket Guide mean by ensemble work?
notes.back: Pairing, swarming or mobbing: lowering WIP below the number of team members so several people work on one item, often an ageing one.
notes.explanation: People who finish an item help the ageing one instead of starting new work, so it makes progress.
notes.example: Two developers who finish their tasks join a colleague on a stuck item rather than pulling new ones.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Pairing, Swarming and Mobbing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is actively managing items in the workflow optional under the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: No. The Guide says items in the workflow must be managed actively.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three practices that work in tandem; none of them is optional.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: The first form of active management the Guide lists is {{c1::controlling WIP}}.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists three forms: controlling WIP, stopping items from ageing unnecessarily, and unblocking blocked work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Which form of active management does the Guide tie to the SLE as its reference?
notes.back: Ensuring work items do not age unnecessarily.
notes.explanation: The SLE says how long an item should take, so it tells you when an item's age is becoming a problem.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: The third form of active management the Guide lists is {{c1::unblocking blocked work}}.
notes.explanation: Blocked items are not flowing but keep ageing, so freeing them is part of managing the work in progress.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Are the Guide's three forms of active management the only ones allowed?
notes.back: No. The Guide says active management can take several forms, including but not limited to the three it lists.
notes.explanation: The list is a minimum set of examples, so teams may manage active items in other ways too.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: How often does the Guide say Kanban system members should review the active items?
notes.back: It sets no fixed cadence: the review can be continuous, at regular intervals, or a combination of both.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls regular review a common practice, not a required meeting.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: The Guide requires the number of items in progress to be controlled {{c1::explicitly}}, not left to chance.
notes.explanation: Kanban system members must explicitly control the number of work items between started and finished.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: How must WIP control be shown on a Kanban board?
notes.back: In any way the Kanban system members deem appropriate; the Guide prescribes no particular form.
notes.explanation: Numbers above columns, slots, tokens or one limit for the whole board all qualify, as long as the control is explicit.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Ideally, should a Kanban system run above or below its agreed WIP control?
notes.back: Neither. Ideally it operates at the agreed control, not above it and not below it.
notes.explanation: Running above the control overloads the system; running well below it can leave capacity idle.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: How does the Guide say a pull system comes about?
notes.back: As an effect of controlling WIP: controlling WIP should create a pull system.
notes.explanation: You don't build pull separately; limiting what is in progress makes new work wait for capacity.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: According to the Guide, what can signal that new work may be selected?
notes.back: WIP dropping below the control set in the DoW.
notes.explanation: That is the clear signal of capacity a pull system waits for.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What should Kanban system members refrain from when selecting work into a part of the workflow?
notes.back: Selecting more work items into it than its WIP control allows.
notes.explanation: Selecting beyond the control breaks the pull system and lets WIP grow unchecked.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Besides helping workflow, which three things does the Guide say controlling WIP often improves?
notes.back: The Kanban system members' collective focus, commitment and collaboration.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives no reason. ProKanban's playbook notes that too many items in progress split people's attention.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6; ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 2.5, “Why should we control WIP?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Guide); C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words (playbook)

notes.front: Where should any acceptable exceptions to WIP control be made explicit?
notes.back: As part of the DoW.
notes.explanation: An exception that lives only in someone's head is not an explicit policy, so nobody can apply it consistently.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Does Kanban require a WIP limit on every column of the board?
notes.back: No. WIP can be controlled in many ways: one limit for the board, per person, for grouped columns, or per column.
notes.explanation: The DoW must say how WIP is controlled, but the way it is implemented is up to the team.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 4 “Controlling WIP”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can you find a board's WIP by adding up its WIP limits?
notes.back: No. Columns are seldom exactly at their limits and limits are often broken, so you must count the items actually in progress.
notes.explanation: WIP is a count of real items; the limits only say what the team intended.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Work In Progress”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does setting WIP limits guarantee that WIP is actually limited?
notes.back: No. The Pocket Guide notes that many teams set WIP limits and then routinely break them.
notes.explanation: A limit on the board controls nothing unless the team keeps to it.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Kanban Systems”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What two ways does the Kanban Pocket Guide give to stop an item from ageing unnecessarily?
notes.back: Finish it, or don't start it.
notes.explanation: An item that is finished no longer ages, and one that is not started has not begun to age; doing both amounts to controlling WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 1 “How To Prevent Work Items From Aging”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Kanban Pocket Guide say is the real reason to control WIP?
notes.back: To prevent work items from ageing unnecessarily.
notes.explanation: Longer age delays customer feedback and raises the risk of spending a long time on something that turns out not to be valuable.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 1 “How To Prevent Work Items From Aging”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When an item is taking too long, what does the Pocket Guide call the most likely culprit?
notes.back: The item is probably too big; look for ways to break it into smaller items that are each still valuable.
notes.explanation: Its age is the best signal that an item may be too big.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 1 “How To Prevent Work Items From Aging”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the first blocked-work policy the Pocket Guide says a team should establish?
notes.back: When to mark an item as blocked: how long its progress must be stopped (hours, days or weeks) first.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide says there are at least three such policies; the others it names cover WIP limits and removing blocked items.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Unblocking Blocked Work”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which blocked-work policy decides whether a blocked item still counts towards the WIP limit?
notes.back: The 'blocked items and WIP limits' policy: how long a blocked item keeps counting towards the WIP limit, stopping new work being pulled.
notes.explanation: Counting it can increase the team's focus on resolving the blocker.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Unblocking Blocked Work”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the third blocked-work policy in the Pocket Guide?
notes.back: When to remove a long-blocked item from the system, for example by cancelling it or moving it back to the backlog.
notes.explanation: An item blocked for long enough may no longer be worth tracking as work in progress.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Unblocking Blocked Work”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Must all work items be the same size for a WIP-controlled system to work?
notes.back: No. Variation in item size always exists; the Pocket Guide says items need to be right-sized, not same-sized.
notes.explanation: The system must cope with varying sizes, within the range the SLE describes.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Right Sizing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the three ways the Pocket Guide says ensemble work helps control age?
notes.back: Doing later-stage steps early; splitting the item's tasks among people; bringing in fresh eyes to get past a sticking point.
notes.explanation: Each helps an item that has aged more than others to keep moving.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Pairing, Swarming and Mobbing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team swarms on an item that has passed its SLE and chases a supplier who is holding up another. Which Kanban practice is this?
notes.back: Actively managing items in a workflow.
notes.choices:
A) Defining and visualizing a workflow
B) Actively managing items in a workflow
C) Improving a workflow
notes.choicesExplained: A: they are not changing what the workflow is or how it is shown. C: they are not changing the DoW; they are acting on items already in progress.
notes.explanation: Keeping items from ageing and unblocking blocked work are both listed forms of active management.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A developer sees an item's age nearing the team's SLE and asks two colleagues to help finish it. Which listed form of active management is this?
notes.back: Ensuring work items do not age unnecessarily, using the SLE as a reference.
notes.explanation: The SLE is the reference that tells the team the item is getting too old.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A team's policy says: anything waiting over a day on another team is flagged and raised with that team's lead. Which listed form of active management does this serve?
notes.back: Unblocking blocked work.
notes.explanation: Flagging and escalating dependencies helps blocked items start flowing again.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A manager says the Kanban Guide requires a Kanban team to hold a daily 15-minute meeting. Is that right?
notes.back: No. The Guide requires no meeting; reviewing active items can be continuous, at regular intervals, or both.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, a daily review meeting is mandatory
B) No, the Guide sets no required meeting or cadence
C) Yes, but only while WIP is above the control
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide calls regular review a common practice, not a requirement, and names no meeting. C: the Guide links no meeting to the WIP level.
notes.explanation: Daily meetings come from other approaches; the Kanban Guide leaves the form of review to the members.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A team's DoW sets a WIP control of 4. Four items are in progress, and a stakeholder asks for a fifth to start now. What does the Guide point to?
notes.back: Wait until WIP drops below the control, unless an exception made explicit in the DoW applies.
notes.choices:
A) Start it: stakeholder requests override the control
B) Wait for WIP to drop below the control, unless an explicit exception in the DoW applies
C) Raise the control to 5 for this item only, without recording it
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says members should refrain from selecting beyond the WIP control. C: the Guide says exceptions should be made explicit as part of the DoW, not improvised.
notes.explanation: The drop below the control is the signal to select new work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Week after week a team has 2 items in progress against an agreed WIP control of 6. Is that the ideal the Guide describes?
notes.back: No. Ideally the system operates neither above nor below the agreed control.
notes.explanation: Consistently running far below the control suggests the control or the way work is selected needs a look.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A manager assigns each new request to someone the moment it arrives, whatever they are already working on. Is this push or pull?
notes.back: Push: work starts whenever it is requested, not when there is a clear signal of capacity.
notes.choicesExplained: A: in a pull system, work is selected only when there is a clear signal that there is capacity to do it.
notes.explanation: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams contrasts pull with a push system, which starts work on an item whenever it is requested.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (Scrum.org, January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”

notes.front: After a team starts controlling WIP, people start helping each other finish items instead of each starting their own. Which benefit named in the Guide is this?
notes.back: Improved collaboration.
notes.explanation: The Guide says controlling WIP often improves collective focus, commitment and collaboration.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A team lets urgent production fixes bypass its WIP control, but the rule exists only in the team lead's head. What does the Guide say the team should do?
notes.back: Make the exception explicit as part of the DoW.
notes.explanation: The Guide says acceptable exceptions to controlling WIP should be made explicit as part of the DoW, so everyone applies them the same way.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Which of these three boards meets the Kanban Guide's rule on controlling WIP?
notes.back: All three: the Guide lets members represent WIP control in any way they deem appropriate.
notes.explanation: Per-column limits, one board limit and a grouped limit are all ways to control WIP explicitly.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A board has WIP limits of 3, 3 and 2 on its three in-progress columns. A manager reports the team's WIP as 8. Is that sound?
notes.back: No. WIP is the count of items actually in progress; columns may be under or over their limits.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide warns that adding up WIP limits does not give you WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Work In Progress”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team's SLE is “85% of items finish in 12 days or less”. A new item looks like three weeks of work. What does right-sizing suggest?
notes.back: Break it up or redefine it before pulling it in, so that it can likely finish within 12 days.
notes.explanation: The right size is the range the SLE describes: here, 12 days or less.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 3 “Right Sizing Redux”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between WIP, WIP control and a WIP limit?
notes.back: WIP is a count of items in progress; WIP control is the required policy; a WIP limit is one optional way to express it.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires WIP to be controlled but does not require WIP limits.
notes.contrast: Count versus rule versus one form of the rule.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What is the difference between actively managing items and improving the workflow?
notes.back: Active management acts on the items in progress now; improving the workflow changes the DoW itself.
notes.explanation: Swarming on an old item is active management; changing a policy or state in the DoW is improvement.
notes.contrast: Acting on the work versus changing how the work flows.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7
